Exponentially Handsome Proof Nets and Their Normalization
Matteo Acclavio

Abstract
Handsome proof nets were introduced by Retoré as a syntax for multiplicative linear logic. These proof nets are defined by means of cographs (graphs representing formulas) equipped with a vertices partition satisfying simple topological conditions. In this paper we extend this syntax to multiplicative linear logic with units and exponentials. For this purpose we develop a new sound and complete sequent system for the logic, enforcing a stronger notion of proof equivalence with respect to the one usually considered in the literature. We then define combinatorial proofs, a graphical proof system able to capture syntactically the proof equivalence, for the cut-free fragment of the calculus. We conclude the paper by defining the exponentially handsome proof nets as combinatorial proofs with cuts and defining an internal normalization procedure for this syntax.

Introduction

One of the novelties introduced by linear logic
[
16
]
was the syntax of proof nets.
Proof nets are a graphical syntax
[
27
,
28
]
for proofs
able to capture the
proof equivalence
in the multiplicative fragment of linear logic (denoted
\mathsf{MLL}
):
proof nets are canonical representative of equivalent proofs modulo independent rules permutations.
In addition, proof nets are a sound and complete proof system in the sense of
[
10
]
for
\mathsf{MLL}
, since it is possible to check if a graph represents a correct derivation in polynomial time with respect to the size of the graph. This test can be conducted by means of a topological criterion, often refereed to as
correctness criterion

[
16
,
13
,
19
,
45
]
.

Several extensions of proof nets have been proposed to cover multiplicative linear logic with units (
\mathsf{MLL_{u}}
),
but none of them can be considered to be fully satisfactory.
In presence of the units, the correctness criterion requires to add additional edges, called
jumps
, to a proof net in order to connect the gates of the unit
\bot
to an axiom or an unit
\mathsf{1}

[
23
]
.

The quest for a satisfactory syntax for
\mathsf{MLL_{u}}
-proofs has come to an end after the publication of
[
22
]
where is shown that it is not possible to have at the same time a syntax capturing the whole
\mathsf{MLL_{u}}
proof equivalence and a polynomial correctness criterion, unless
\mathsf{P}=\mathsf{NP}
.
This result depends on the presence of the jumps:
on one hand they are needed in order to check in polynomial time if the proof net is correct,
but on the other hand they enforce a coarse notion of proof equivalence which requires to “rewire” the jumps to capture the full proof equivalence.

A similar problem occurs in the multiplicative exponential linear logic (
\mathsf{MELL}
) due to the presence the weakening rule
1
1

1

Indeed, the decidability of
\mathsf{MELL}
is still an open question and depends on the presence of the weakening rule
[
26
,
50
]
.

[
52
,
51
]
.
Moreover, the presence of the promotion rule in this fragment poses an additional difficulty since
this rule is context-sensitive.
However this latter problem is easily addressed by including in the proof net syntax the so called
boxes
whose scope is to delimit portions of the graph
[
36
,
31
,
33
,
4
,
3
]
,
as shown in
Figure

1
.

Upper row
:
a derivation of the sequent
\bar{d},d\mathop{\otimes}(\wn c\invamp\oc a),\wn(\bar{a}\mathop{\otimes}\bar{b}),\wn b

in
\mathsf{MELL}

and a corresponding proof net (with jump drawn as a dotted edge).

Lower row
:
a decomposed derivation in
\mathsf{MELL^{j}}
of the same sequent
and its corresponding exponentially handsome proof net.
In this latter, the gray shadings represent
\mathsf{cut}
-rules, and the vertex
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\circ}
represents the jump.

Handsome proof nets
are an alternative syntax for
\mathsf{MLL}
proofs introduced
by Retoré in
[
40
,
45
]

using the results
from his PhD thesis

[
38
]
.
In this syntax,
the information contained in a proof is represented by specific graphs encoding formulas
(called
cographs
2
2

2

A cograph is a graph containing no induced subgraph isomorph to the four-vertices path
\mathsf{P}_{4}
. In
[
14
]
it is shown that a graph encodes a formula iff it is a cograph.
)
together with a
perfect matching which satisfies specific topological conditions.
For this reason, we this syntax is called
RB-cographs
.

Combinatorial proofs

were introduced by Hughes
[
24
,
25
,
47
]

to capture proof equivalence in classical logic
[
48
,
5
]
.
They can be considered as an extension of handsome proof nets since they are defined as
specific graph homomorphisms from a RB-cograph to a cograph encoding a formula.
In particular, combinatorial proofs indirectly give us a decomposition result,
allowing to separate the “linear” part of the proof, that is,
the part containing the logical interactions between its components,
from
the “resource management” part, that is,
the part taking care of erasing and duplicating components.

Contribution of the paper.

In this paper we extend Retoré’s handsome proof nets for
\mathsf{MLL}

and we define a syntax able to represent proofs in
\mathsf{MLL_{u}}
and
\mathsf{MELL}
.
For this purpose, we define combinatorial proofs
for cut-free
\mathsf{MELL}
-derivations,
and then we show how to also encode derivation with cuts.

To achieve our goal,
we first definite of a new sound and complete proof system for
\mathsf{MELL}
,
called
\mathsf{MELL^{j}}
, and we prove cut-elimination for it.
This system contains the
weak promotion
rule from light linear logic
[
18
,
29
,
32
]

and the
digging rule
instead of regular promotion.
Moreover, the system uniquely assigns each unit
\bot
and each weakening rule to an branch of a derivation thanks to ad-hoc rules.
This choice allows us to mimic jumps assignation in proof nets and reduce the complexity of proof equivalence.

We then extend the results in
[
7
]
in order to define combinatorial proofs for
\mathsf{MELL^{j}}
.
This allows us to represent equivalent cut-free derivations in
\mathsf{MELL^{j}}
.
We show that this syntax has a polynomial correctness criterion and is able to syntactically capture the proof equivalence, that is, equivalent
\mathsf{MELL^{j}}
-derivations are represented by the same syntactic object.

We conclude by defining
exponentially handsome proof nets

as extensions of the combinatorial proofs syntax.
Exponentially handsome proof nets allow us to encode derivations containing cuts, hence to compose proofs.
Finally, we provide a cut-elimination procedure for this syntax by means of a terminating graph rewriting.

Organization of the paper.

In
Section

2

we discuss the notion of proof equivalence for the standard
\mathsf{MELL}
sequent calculus.
Then we define a sound and complete proof system
\mathsf{MELL^{j}}
for
\mathsf{MELL}
,
where
\mathsf{MELL}
-proof equivalence is restricted.
We then prove a decomposition theorem for
\mathsf{MELL^{j}}
using
deep inference rules
[
20
,
21
,
9
]
.
In
Sections

3
,
4
and
5
we define the three components needed to define combinatorial proofs for
\mathsf{MELL^{j}}
.
In particular, in
Section

3
we recall relation webs
[
20
,
8
]
, which generalize cographs, and we show how they can be used to encode formulas with modalities.
In
Section

4
we extend the correctness criterion for Retoré’s RB-cographs
to relation webs with special matchings, called RGB-cographs,
which encode the linear part of a
\mathsf{MELL^{j}}
proof.
In
Section

5
we define the
\mathsf{MELL}
-fibrations
taking care of encoding the resource management part of our proofs.
In
Section

6
we define combinatorial proofs as
\mathsf{MELL}
-fibrations from an RGB-cograph to a relation web.
Finally, in
Section

7
,
we define exponentially handsome proof nets as
\mathsf{MELL}
-combinatorial proofs of sequents containing additional formulas keeping track of the
\mathsf{cut}
-rules,
and we provide a cut-elimination procedure for this syntax.

\mathsf{MELL}

We then discuss in

and in

\mathsf{MELL}
,
enforcing a coarser notion of proof equivalence.
In
Section

2.4
we show that this new proof system admits a decomposition theorem,
which we exploit in
Section

to define the syntax of combinatorial proofs for
\mathsf{MELL}
.

Figure 2:
Sequent calculus rules for
\mathsf{MELL}
and the
\mathsf{cut}
-rule

We define formulas in negation normal form generated from
a countable set of propositional variables
\mathcal{A}=\{a,b,\dots\}

and set of constants
\{\mathsf{1},\bot,{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\circ}\}
3
3

3

The symbols
\bot
and
\mathsf{1}
are called units. The symbol
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\circ}
is a special symbol which we use as a “placeholder” for
\bot
and weakening rules.

by the following grammar:

A,B::=a\mid\bar{a}\mid A\invamp B\mid A\mathop{\otimes}B\mid\oc A\mid\wn A\mid\bot\mid\mathsf{1}\mid{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\circ}

A
literal
is a formula of the shape
a
or
\bar{a}
for an
a\in\mathcal{A}
.
A
\mathsf{MELL}
-formula
is a formula containing no occurrences of
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\circ}
.
Linear negation
\bar{\cdot}
is defined on
\mathsf{MELL}
formulas through the De Morgan laws:

\overline{\overline{A}}=A
,

\overline{A\mathop{\otimes}B}=\overline{A}\invamp\overline{B}
,

\overline{\oc A}=\wn\bar{A}
,

\bar{\mathsf{1}}=\bot
.
A
sequent

\Gamma=A_{1},\dots,A_{n}
is a non-empty multiset of formulas.

In this paper we consider
multiplicative linear logic
and its extensions with

units
and
and
exponentials
4
4

4

In this paper, where not otherwise specified, we consider multiplicative exponential linear logic including units.
denoted respectively by
\mathsf{MLL}
,
\mathsf{MLL_{u}}
and
\mathsf{MELL}

[
16
]
.
We use the same names to denote the cut-free sequent calculi for these logics defined using the sequent calculus rules in Figure
2
.

\mathsf{MLL}=\{\mathsf{ax},\mathop{\otimes},\invamp\}\qquad\mathsf{MLL_{u}}=\mathsf{MLL}\cup\{\bot,\mathsf{1}\}\qquad\mathsf{MELL}=\mathsf{MLL_{u}}\cup\{\mathsf{\oc}p,\mathsf{w}_{\wn},\mathsf{c}_{\wn},\mathsf{der}_{\wn}\}

We say that a formula
F
is provable in
\mathsf{X}
(denoted by
{\mathrel{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathsf{X}}}{{\hbox to15.43pt{\vbox to6.09pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 0.59999pt\lower-3.04544pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{}{{}}{}
{}{}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{}\lxSVG@stroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 0 0 L 19.69 0}{fill:none} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
\lxSVG@closescope {}{{}}{}
{}{}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{}\lxSVG@stroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 0 -3.94 L 0 3.94}{fill:none} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
\lxSVG@closescope }
\lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}}}}F}
) if there is a derivation of
F
in the system
\mathsf{X}
.

We recall the cut-elimination result for
\mathsf{MELL}
, which encompasses also
\mathsf{MLL}
and
\mathsf{MLL_{u}}
.

Theorem 1

(
[
16
]
)
.

Let
F
be a formula.
Then
F
is provable in
\mathsf{MELL}
iff it is provable in
\mathsf{MELL}\cup\{\mathsf{cut}\}
.

2.1
From Proof Nets to Handsome Proof Nets

Proof nets
are a graphical syntax for proofs in linear logic introduced by Girard in
[
16
]
.
In this syntax,
\mathsf{MLL}
proofs are represented by
replacing each instance of a rule
by a corresponding
gate

whose
inputs are the active formulas of the rule
and
whose
outputs are the principal formulas, as shown in the upper row of
Figure

3
.
The graphs generated by these gates are called
proof structures
and some of them do not have a corresponding proof in
\mathsf{MLL}
.
Therefore, a topological
correctness criterion
needs to be defined to decide whether a proof structure is a proof net, i.e., is the translation of a
\mathsf{MLL}
proof.
Beside Girard’s
duable trip condition
,
several alternative criteria have been proposed in the literature

[
13
,
19
]
.

Using
RB-graphs
,
which are graphs with two kind of edges
(
Red
or Regular, and
Blue
or Bold),
Retoré defined in
[
40
]

the syntax of

RB-proof nets

where gates are represented as the RB-graphs, as shown in the lower row of
Figure

3
.
In this syntax the correctness criterion can be formulated by requiring the absence of elementary (i.e., non self-intersecting) cycles made of alternating colours edges.
From RB-proof nets,
he then discovered the syntax of

handsome proof nets
(or
RB-cographs
)
by using the transformation in
Equation

1
below,
allowing to remove from an RB-graph
all the nodes which are not labelled by literals
[
40
,
41
,
45
]
.
This syntax is formally presented in
Section

4
.
Aim of this paper is to further develop RB-cographs by adding an encoding of the linear logic modalities and units.

The encodings for modalities we employ in this paper uses the same kind of directed edges from
the handsome proof nets for

pomset logic

[
39
,
8
,
42
,
43
,
45
,
44
]

(we here represent these edges by green squiggly arrows instead of red arrows).
The upper row of the rightmost column of
Figure

3
shows
the usual encoding of the promotion rule of
\mathsf{MELL}
by means of
boxes
isolating a portion of the proof net.
In the lower row of the same column
we provide the intuitive representation
of how the same box should be represented
in terms of the RB-proof nets.
This intuition might help the reader familiar with proof nets; however, it is not further developed in the paper, as our approach focuses on generalizing RB-cographs.

Figure 5:
Additional rules permutations.
The first line is called the
weakening-contraction comonad

.

The notion of
proof equivalence
in
\mathsf{MELL}
is defined (e.g., in
[
37
,
12
]
) as the equivalence relation
\simeq
over
\mathsf{MELL}
-derivations generated by
independent rules permutations
, i.e.,
the permutations of rules which have disjoint sets of principal and active formulas shown in
Figure

4
, together with the ones in
Figure

5
.
It is worth noticing that these rules permutations are heavily used in the proof of cut-elimination theorems.

As shown in
[
22
]
, the instances of rule permutations in the last line of
Figure

4
involving
\mathsf{\bot}
-rule
are responsible of
the
\mathsf{P}
-
\mathsf{space}
complexity bound of checking proof equivalence in
\mathsf{MLL_{u}}
.
In fact, these rules permutations allows to move the
\bot
formula between different derivation branchings as shown in the following example,
where the leftmost and rightmost derivations, which are equivalent, are “naturally” represented by two different proof nets.

As consequence of this complexity result, we cannot design a syntax
\mathcal{S}
for
\mathsf{MLL_{u}}
satisfying the two following desiderata at the same time under the assumption
\mathsf{P}\neq\mathsf{NP}
:

•

correctedness in
\mathcal{S}
can be checked in polynomial time:
we can check in polynomial time if an object expressed in the syntax
\mathcal{S}
represents a correct proof in
\mathsf{MLL_{u}}
;

•

\mathcal{S}
captures proof equivalence:
if
{\llbracket\pi\rrbracket}
and
{\llbracket\pi^{\prime}\rrbracket}
are the encodings in
\mathcal{S}
of two derivations
\pi
and
\pi^{\prime}
in
\mathsf{MELL}
such that
\pi\simeq\pi^{\prime}
, then
{\llbracket\pi\rrbracket}={\llbracket\pi^{\prime}\rrbracket}
.

The same argument applies to
\mathsf{MELL}
-derivations in presence of the rule
\mathsf{w}_{\wn}
.
The complexity of checking proof equivalence depends on the fact that each
\mathsf{w}_{\wn}
and
\mathsf{\bot}
must be assigned to an instance of
\mathsf{ax}
or of
\mathsf{1}
by permuting them upwards in a derivation. We refer to such assignation as
jump
.
Since
\simeq
allows to re-assign jumps, the equivalence check has to test all possible jumps, whose number is exponential with respect to the number of
\mathsf{\bot}
and
\mathsf{w}_{\wn}
in a derivation.

As consequence of
[
22
]
,
we cannot aspire to design a proof system
5
5

5

In the sense of
[
10
]
, that is, in which we can check if a syntactic object is correct in polynomial time.

which captures the proof equivalence
\simeq
of
\mathsf{MELL}
.
To overcome this problem,
in this subsection
we define
\mathsf{MELL^{j}}
, a sound and complete proof system for
\mathsf{MELL}

enforcing a coarser proof equivalence, denoted by
\simeq_{\mathsf{J}}
, with respect to
\simeq
.
In fact, in
\mathsf{MELL^{j}}
each
\mathsf{\bot}
- and
\mathsf{w}_{\wn}
-rule instance
is uniquely associated to a specific
\mathsf{ax}
- or
\mathsf{1}
-rule instance,
mimicking the way in which the corresponding nodes are linked by jumps in a proof net.

We define the following sequent systems using the rules in
Figures

2
and
6

\mathsf{MLL_{u}^{j}}=\{\mathsf{ax}_{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}j}},\mathsf{1}_{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}j}},{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\bot^{\mathsf{j}}},\invamp,\mathop{\otimes}\}\qquad\mathsf{MELL^{j}}=\{\mathsf{ax}_{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}j}},\mathsf{1}_{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}j}},{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\bot^{\mathsf{j}}},{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathsf{w^{j}}},\invamp,\mathop{\otimes},\mathsf{w}\oc p,\mathsf{der}_{\wn},\mathsf{dig}_{\wn},\mathsf{dig}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\circ},\mathsf{c}_{\wn}\}

where
\mathsf{ax}_{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}j}}=\{\mathsf{ax}_{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}j}}^{n}\mid n\in\mathbb{N}\}
and
\mathsf{1}_{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}j}}=\{\mathsf{1}_{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}j}}^{n}\mid n\in\mathbb{N}\}
.
The proof equivalence
\simeq_{\mathsf{J}}
over
\mathsf{MELL^{j}}
derivations is defined as in
Figure

4
by considering
\rho
and
\tau
ranging over
\{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\bot^{\mathsf{j}}},{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathsf{w^{j}}},\invamp,\mathsf{der}_{\wn},\mathsf{dig}_{\wn},\mathsf{dig}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\circ},\mathsf{c}_{\wn}\}

plus the
associativity of contraction
, that is, the rule permutation in the left-hand side of
Figure

5
.

In these systems the relation between one
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\bot^{\mathsf{j}}}
- or
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathsf{w^{j}}}
-rule and one
\mathsf{ax}_{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}j}}
- or
\mathsf{1}_{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}j}}
-rule is
syntactically encoded in the sequent system syntax, as jumps in proof nets are.
Each instance of
\mathsf{ax}_{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}j}}
and
\mathsf{1}_{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}j}}
introduces a bunch of jump place-holders denoted by
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\circ}
.
Since each occurrence of a
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\circ}
is unique, each place-holder is further used by a single
\mathsf{\bot}
or
\mathsf{w}_{\wn}
instance.

Remark 2
.

Another solution to uniquely associate
\mathsf{\bot}
and
\mathsf{w}_{\wn}
to an axiom
would be to introduce an axiom rule with non-empty contexts, i.e.,
a rule having as conclusion any sequent of the shape
\Gamma,a,\bar{a}
,
as done in sequent calculus for classical logic
\mathsf{G}

[
53
]
.
Such axiom rule would keep track of whole information of the weakened formula,
making the syntax of the structures described in
Section

4
heavier.

Moreover, in
\mathsf{MELL^{j}}
we replace the
promotion
rule
\mathsf{\oc}p
with the
weak promotion
rule
\mathsf{w}\oc p
used in
light linear logic

[
18
]
and in
soft linear logic

[
29
,
32
]
and the
digging
rule.
This choice is motivated by the fact that weak promotion allows to group the
\oc
introduced by a promotion with all the
\wn
of its context formulas.
In particular, weak promotion is a context-free rule, that is, it can be applied independently form the shape of the premise context,
while the regular promotion rule
\mathsf{\oc}p
is a context-sensitive rule, in the sense that it can be applied only if the context is of the form
\wn\Gamma
.
The digging rules
\mathsf{dig}_{\wn}
and
\mathsf{dig}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\circ}
are required to make the system sound and complete with respect to
\mathsf{MELL}
.

Figure 7:
How to transform a
\mathsf{\bot}
associate to a specific
\mathsf{ax}
-rule to a
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\bot^{\mathsf{j}}}
associate to a
\mathsf{ax}_{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}j}}
-rule, and how to replace
\mathsf{\oc}p
with a derivation using
\mathsf{w}\oc p
and
\mathsf{dig}_{\wn}
and vice versa. Note that elimination of the
\mathsf{dig}_{\wn}
introduces a
\mathsf{cut}
, which can be eliminated relying on the cut-elimination result in
\mathsf{MELL}
.

Theorem 3
.

If
F
is a fomula, then

\mathrel{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathsf{X}}}{{\hbox to15.43pt{\vbox to6.09pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 0.59999pt\lower-3.04544pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{}{{}}{}

\lxSVG@closescope {}{{}}{}
{}{}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{}\lxSVG@stroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 0 -3.94 L 0 3.94}{fill:none} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
\lxSVG@closescope }

iff
\mathrel{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathsf{X}^{j}}}{{\hbox to15.43pt{\vbox to6.09pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 0.59999pt\lower-3.04544pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{}{{}}{}

.

Proof.

By rules permutations, we can move each occurrence
\rho
of a
\mathsf{w}_{\wn}
- or a
\mathsf{\bot}
-rule up in the derivation until it reaches the assigned occurrence
\sigma_{\rho}
of an
\mathsf{ax}_{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}j}}
- or a
\mathsf{1}_{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}j}}
-rule.
Then we replace
\sigma_{\rho}
with an occurrence of the same rule
\sigma_{\rho}
with an additional
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\circ}
in the conclusion, and
\rho
with an occurrence of
\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\rho^{\mathsf{j}}

applied to this fresh
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\circ}
(an example is shown in Figure
7
).
Moreover, every
\mathsf{\oc}p
can be replaced by a
\mathsf{w}\oc p
followed by a finite number of
\mathsf{dig}_{\wn}
and vice versa by
\mathsf{MELL}
cut-elimination theorem
[
16
]
(see Figure
7
).
∎

Strictly speaking, the proof system
\mathsf{MELL^{j}}
does not satisfy the
subformula property
because of the presence of the rules
\mathsf{dig}_{\wn}
and
\mathsf{dig}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\circ}
.
However, we can prove a cut-elimination result.
Observe that a weaker notion of the subformula property holds since all formulas that can appear in a derivation of an arbitrary sequent are going to be subformulas of a formula at the root or formulas of the form
\wn\cdots\wn A
where
\wn A
is a subformula of a formula at the root.
At the moment this paper is written, the decidability of
\mathsf{MELL}
is an open question
[
50
]
.
Thus we do not focus on proof search for
\mathsf{MELL^{j}}
.

, where
\rho_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}j}\in\{\mathsf{ax}_{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}j}},\mathsf{1}_{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}j}}\}

involved in the cut-elimination step.

3
Relation Webs

Cographs
are graphs encoding formulas constructed using a conjunction and a disjunction connective
[
14
]
.
In this section we present
modal relation webs
, which generalize cographs, and which will be used in the next sections to encode
\mathsf{MELL}
-formulas
We define modal relation webs as mixed graphs (i.e., graphs with both directed and undirected edges) satisfying certain topological conditions.
Moreover, we show that they identify formulas modulo associativity and commutativity of
\mathop{\otimes}
and
\invamp
.

A
directed graph

\mathcal{G}=\langle V_{\mathcal{G}},\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathcal{G}}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.25,0.16}\rightsquigarrow}}}}\mkern 1.0mu\rangle
is a set

V_{\mathcal{G}}
of
vertices
equipped with an irreflexive binary
edge relation

\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathcal{G}}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.25,0.16}\rightsquigarrow}}}}\mkern 1.0mu\subseteq V_{\mathcal{G}}\times V_{\mathcal{G}}
.
An

undirected graph

\mathcal{G}=\langle V_{\mathcal{G}},\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathcal{G}}}{{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\frown}}}}\mkern 1.0mu\rangle
is a graph whose

edge relation

\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathcal{G}}}{{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\frown}}}}\mkern 1.0mu\subseteq V_{\mathcal{G}}\times V_{\mathcal{G}}
is
irreflexive and symmetric. A
mixed graph
is a triple

\mathcal{G}=\langle V_{\mathcal{G}},\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathcal{G}}}{{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\frown}}}}\mkern 1.0mu,\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathcal{G}}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.25,0.16}\rightsquigarrow}}}}\mkern 1.0mu\rangle
where

\langle V_{\mathcal{G}},\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathcal{G}}}{{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\frown}}}}\mkern 1.0mu\rangle
is an undirected graph and

\langle V_{\mathcal{G}},\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathcal{G}}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.25,0.16}\rightsquigarrow}}}}\mkern 1.0mu\rangle
is a directed graph, such that

\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathcal{G}}}{{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\frown}}}}\mkern 1.0mu\cap\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathcal{G}}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.25,0.16}\rightsquigarrow}}}}\mkern 1.0mu=\emptyset
and
\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathcal{G}}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.25,0.16}\rightsquigarrow}}}}\mkern 1.0mu
is irreflexive.
We omit the
index/superscript
\mathcal{G}
when it is clear from the context.
When drawing a graph we draw
\mathord{\hbox to5.21pt{\vbox to4.31pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 2.603pt\lower-2.15277pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{}}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\hbox{\hbox{{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{}{}{{

{}{}}
{{}{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}}{{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}{}{{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces

A mixed graph is
\mathcal{L}
-labeled
if each vertex
v
carries a label
l(v)
selected from a label set
\mathcal{L}
.
In this paper we fix the label set to be
\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{A}\cup\bar{\mathcal{A}}\cup\{\oc,\wn,\mathsf{1},\bot,{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\circ}\}
.

Definition 6
.

A
relation web
is a non-empty mixed graph

\mathcal{G}=\langle V_{\mathcal{G}},\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathcal{G}}}{{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\frown}}}}\mkern 1.0mu,\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathcal{G}}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.25,0.16}\rightsquigarrow}}}}\mkern 1.0mu\rangle

such that:

•

\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathcal{G}}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.25,0.16}\rightsquigarrow}}}}\mkern 1.0mu
is transitive and irreflexive;

•

\langle V_{\mathcal{G}},\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathcal{G}}}{{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\frown}}}}\mkern 1.0mu\rangle
is a
cograph
,
\langle V_{\mathcal{G}},\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathcal{G}}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.25,0.16}\rightsquigarrow}}}}\mkern 1.0mu\rangle
is a
series-parallel order
and
\mathcal{G}
is
3-color triangle-free
,
that is,
\mathcal{G}
contains no induced subgraphs of the following shape:

(3)

A
cograph
is an undirected graph containing no induced subgraph as the leftmost one in
Equation

3
.

Let
\mathcal{G}
and
\mathcal{H}
be two disjoint mixed graphs. We define the following operations:

\hss\begin{array}[]{c@{\;\;=\;\;}l}\mathcal{G}\invamp\mathcal{H}&\mathchoice{\hbox{$\displaystyle{\langle V_{\mathcal{G}}\cup V_{\mathcal{H}}\;,\;\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathcal{G}}}{{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\frown}}}}\mkern 1.0mu\cup\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathcal{H}}}{{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\frown}}}}\mkern 1.0mu\;,\;\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathcal{G}}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.25,0.16}\rightsquigarrow}}}}\mkern 1.0mu\cup\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathcal{H}}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.25,0.16}\rightsquigarrow}}}}\mkern 1.0mu\rangle}$}}{\hbox{$\textstyle{\langle V_{\mathcal{G}}\cup V_{\mathcal{H}}\;,\;\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathcal{G}}}{{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\frown}}}}\mkern 1.0mu\cup\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathcal{H}}}{{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\frown}}}}\mkern 1.0mu\;,\;\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathcal{G}}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.25,0.16}\rightsquigarrow}}}}\mkern 1.0mu\cup\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathcal{H}}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.25,0.16}\rightsquigarrow}}}}\mkern 1.0mu\rangle}$}}{\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\langle V_{\mathcal{G}}\cup V_{\mathcal{H}}\;,\;\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathcal{G}}}{{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\frown}}}}\mkern 1.0mu\cup\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathcal{H}}}{{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\frown}}}}\mkern 1.0mu\;,\;\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathcal{G}}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.25,0.16}\rightsquigarrow}}}}\mkern 1.0mu\cup\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathcal{H}}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.25,0.16}\rightsquigarrow}}}}\mkern 1.0mu\rangle}$}}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\langle V_{\mathcal{G}}\cup \mathcal{G}\mathbin{\vartriangleleft}\mathcal{H}&\langle V_{\mathcal{G}}\cup V_{\mathcal{H}}\;,\;\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathcal{G}}}{{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\frown}}}}\mkern 1.0mu\cup\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathcal{H}}}{{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\frown}}}}\mkern 1.0mu\;,\;\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathcal{G}}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.25,0.16}\rightsquigarrow}}}}\mkern 1.0mu\cup\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathcal{H}}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.25,0.16}\rightsquigarrow}}}}\mkern 1.0mu\cup\{(u,v)\mid u\in V_{\mathcal{G}},v\in V_{\mathcal{H}}\}\rangle\\

Theorem 7

(
[
20
,
8
]
)
.

A mixed graph is a relation web if and only if it can be constructed from single vertices using the three operations
\invamp
,
\mathbin{\vartriangleleft}
and
\mathop{\otimes}
defined in
Equation

4
.

For each formula
F
we define the
\mathcal{L}
-labeled relation web
{\llbracket F\rrbracket}
.
We use the notations
\scriptstyle{a}
,
\scriptstyle{\bar{a}}
,
{\scriptstyle\oc}
,

{\scriptstyle\wn}
,
{\scriptstyle 1}
,
{\scriptstyle\bot}
and
{\scriptstyle{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\circ}}
for the graph consisting of a single vertex
that is labeled with
a
,
\bar{a}
,
\oc
,
\wn
,
\mathsf{1}
,
\bot
and
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\circ}
respectively.

\hskip 3.00003pt\begin{array}[]{c@{\;\;=\;\;}l}{\llbracket a\rrbracket}&\scriptstyle{a}\\
{\llbracket\bar{a}\rrbracket}&\scriptstyle{\bar{a}}\end{array}\hskip 15.00002pt\begin{array}[]{c@{\;\;=\;\;}l}{\llbracket A\mathop{\otimes}B\rrbracket}&{\llbracket A\rrbracket}\mathop{\otimes}{\llbracket B\rrbracket}\\
{\llbracket A\invamp B\rrbracket}&{\llbracket A\rrbracket}\invamp{\llbracket B\rrbracket}\end{array}\hskip 15.00002pt\begin{array}[]{c@{\;\;=\;\;}l}{\llbracket\oc A\rrbracket}&{\scriptstyle\oc}\mathbin{\vartriangleleft}{\llbracket A\rrbracket}\\
{\llbracket\wn A\rrbracket}&{\scriptstyle\wn}\mathbin{\vartriangleleft}{\llbracket A\rrbracket}\end{array}\hskip 15.00002pt\begin{array}[]{c@{\;\;=\;\;}l}{\llbracket\mathsf{1}\rrbracket}&{\scriptstyle 1}\\
{\llbracket\bot\rrbracket}&{\scriptstyle\bot}\end{array}\hskip 15.00002pt\begin{array}[]{c@{\;\;=\;\;}l}{\llbracket{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\circ}\rrbracket}&{\scriptstyle{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\circ}}\\
\end{array}

(5)

For a sequent
\Gamma=A_{1},\ldots,A_{n}
we define
{\llbracket\Gamma\rrbracket}={\llbracket A_{1},\ldots,A_{n}\rrbracket}={\llbracket A_{1}\rrbracket}\invamp\cdots\invamp{\llbracket A_{n}\rrbracket}
.

Definition 8
.

A relation web
\mathcal{G}
is
properly labeled
if for each
v,w\in V_{\mathcal{G}}
we have
v\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.25,0.16}\rightsquigarrow}}}}\mkern 1.0muw
iff
l(v)\in\{\oc,\wn\}
.

Moreover, we say that a relation web
\mathcal{G}
is
modal
if it is properly labeled and for any vertices
u
,
v
,

w
with
u\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.25,0.16}\rightsquigarrow}}}}\mkern 1.0muw
and
v\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.25,0.16}\rightsquigarrow}}}}\mkern 1.0muw
we have
u\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.25,0.16}\rightsquigarrow}}}}\mkern 1.0muv
or
v\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.25,0.16}\rightsquigarrow}}}}\mkern 1.0muu
or
u=v
, i.e.,
\mathcal{G}
does not contain the two configurations below.

(6)

By adapting the proofs in
[
7
]
, we have the following results:

Theorem 9
.

A relation web is the translation of a formula iff
it is modal.

Proof.

If
\mathcal{G}={\llbracket F\rrbracket}
for some formula
F
, then each vertex with an outgoing
\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.25,0.16}\rightsquigarrow}}}}\mkern 1.0mu
-edge is the encoding of the modality of a subformula of
F
, hence such vertex is labeled with
\oc
or
\wn
.
Moreover, if two distinct such vertices
u
and
v
have a
\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.25,0.16}\rightsquigarrow}}}}\mkern 1.0mu
-edge to some vertex
w
, then that
w
is the encoding of a modality or an atom occurring in a subformula in the scope of the modalities corresponding to
u
and
v
. Thus one of such modalities is in the scope of the other and we have
u\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.25,0.16}\rightsquigarrow}}}}\mkern 1.0muv
or
v\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.25,0.16}\rightsquigarrow}}}}\mkern 1.0muu
.
The converse follows from Theorem
7
and the fact that the operation
\mathbin{\vartriangleleft}
in
Equation

4
is associative.
∎

If
\mathcal{G}
is a modal relation web, we denote by
V^{\bullet}_{\mathcal{G}}
,
V^{\scriptstyle 1}_{\mathcal{G}}
,
V^{\scriptstyle{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\circ}}_{\mathcal{G}}
,
V^{\scriptstyle\oc}_{\mathcal{G}}
and
V^{\scriptstyle\wn}_{\mathcal{G}}
the set of vertices in
V_{\mathcal{G}}
with labels respectively in
\mathcal{A}\cup\bar{\mathcal{A}}
,
\{\mathsf{1}\}
,
\{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\circ}\}
,
\{\oc\}
and
\{\wn\}
.
We call
atomic
,
unit
,
jump
, and
modal
vertices the ones respectively in
V^{\bullet}_{\mathcal{G}}
,
V^{\scriptstyle 1}_{\mathcal{G}}
,
V^{\scriptstyle{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\circ}}_{\mathcal{G}}
, and
V^{{\scriptstyle\oc}{\scriptstyle\wn}}_{\mathcal{G}}=V^{\scriptstyle\oc}_{\mathcal{G}}\cup V^{\scriptstyle\wn}_{\mathcal{G}}
.

Proposition 10
.

Given a set
V_{\mathcal{G}}
and two binary edge relations
\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathcal{G}}}{{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\frown}}}}\mkern 1.0mu
and
\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathcal{G}}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.25,0.16}\rightsquigarrow}}}}\mkern 1.0mu
on vertices
it can be checked in time polynomial on the size
\left|V_{\mathcal{G}}\right|
, whether
\mathcal{G}=\langle V_{\mathcal{G}},\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathcal{G}}}{{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\frown}}}}\mkern 1.0mu,\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathcal{G}}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.25,0.16}\rightsquigarrow}}}}\mkern 1.0mu\rangle
is a modal relation web.

Proof.

Checking the transitivity and irreflexivity of
\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathcal{G}}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.25,0.16}\rightsquigarrow}}}}\mkern 1.0mu
and symmetry of
\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathcal{G}}}{{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\frown}}}}\mkern 1.0mu

is polynomial on
\left|V_{\mathcal{G}}\right|
.
Then, to check the absence of the forbidden configurations in (
3
) and (
6
)
we just check all triples and quadruples of vertices, which is
\mathbf{O}(\left|V_{\mathcal{G}}\right|^{4})
.
Checking the property of being properly labeled is liner on
\left|V_{\mathcal{G}}\right|
.
∎

By associativity of the graph operations
\invamp
,
\mathop{\otimes}
and
\mathbin{\vartriangleleft}
in
Equation

4
and the commutativity of
\invamp
and
\mathop{\otimes}
we have the following equivalence.

Proposition 11
.

For two formulas
F
and
F^{\prime}
, we have
{\llbracket F\rrbracket}={\llbracket F^{\prime}\rrbracket}

iff
F
and
F^{\prime}
are equivalent modulo associativity of and
commutativity of
\mathop{\otimes}
and
\invamp
.

4
RGB-Cographs

As discussed in
Section

2.1
, RB-cograph are an alternative syntax for
\mathsf{MLL}
proof nets.
In this paper we consider
RGB-cographs from
[
7
]
,
which are an extension of the RB-cograph syntax.
We provide a further extension of RGB-cographs and we establish
a correspondence between these graphs and
\mathsf{MELL}^{\ell}
-proofs.

Definition 12
.

An
RGB-cograph
is a tuple

\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathcal{G}=\langle V_{\mathcal{G}},\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathcal{G}}}{{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\frown}}}}\mkern 1.0mu,\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathcal{G}}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.25,0.16}\rightsquigarrow}}}}\mkern 1.0mu,\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathcal{G}}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\curlyvee}}}}\mkern 1.0mu\rangle

where

\lfloor{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathcal{G}}\rfloor=\langle V_{\mathcal{G}},\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathcal{G}}}{{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\frown}}}}\mkern 1.0mu,\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathcal{G}}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.25,0.16}\rightsquigarrow}}}}\mkern 1.0mu\rangle
is a modal relation web,
and
\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathcal{G}}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\curlyvee}}}}\mkern 1.0mu
is an equivalence relation over
V_{\mathcal{G}}
, called the
linking
, such that

•

if
v\in V^{\bullet}_{\mathcal{G}}
then there is exactly another
w\in V^{\bullet}_{\mathcal{G}}
with
v\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\curlyvee}}}}\mkern 1.0muw
and
v\neq w
;

•

if
v\in V^{\scriptstyle 1}_{\mathcal{G}}
then
w\in V^{\scriptstyle{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\circ}}_{\mathcal{G}}
for all
w\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\curlyvee}}}}\mkern 1.0muv
such that
w\neq v
;

•

if
v\in V^{\scriptstyle{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\circ}}_{\mathcal{G}}
then there is a
u\in V^{\bullet}_{\mathcal{G}}\cup V^{\scriptstyle 1}_{\mathcal{G}}
such that
w\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\curlyvee}}}}\mkern 1.0muv
;

•

if
v\in V^{\scriptstyle\oc}_{\mathcal{G}}\cup V^{\scriptstyle\wn}_{\mathcal{G}}
then there is a unique
w\in V^{\scriptstyle\oc}_{\mathcal{G}}
such that
w\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\curlyvee}}}}\mkern 1.0muv
and no
w\in V^{\scriptstyle{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\circ}}_{\mathcal{G}}
such that
w\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\curlyvee}}}}\mkern 1.0muv
;

In particular, an
RB-cograph
is an RGB-cograph
\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathcal{G}
with
V_{\mathcal{G}}=V^{\bullet}_{\mathcal{G}}
.

These conditions can be interpreted as follows:
the jumps vertices are associated to either to a pair of atomic vertices or to a single unit vertex;
modal vertices are grouped in classes containing a unique vertex in
V^{\scriptstyle\oc}_{\mathcal{G}}
.
For readers familiar with proof nets syntax,

{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\circ}
-vertices can be seen as
placeholders for the proof net jumps
while
the
\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\curlyvee}}}}\mkern 1.0mu
-classes containing
\oc
and
\wn
-vertices can be thought as encoding borders of boxes, where the unique
\oc
-vertex is the box principal ports and the
\wn
-vertices are the auxiliary ports.
More precisely, the content of the box delimited by a
\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\curlyvee}}}}\mkern 1.0mu
-class is the induced suggraph containing all the vertices
v
such that
w\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.25,0.16}\rightsquigarrow}}}}\mkern 1.0muv
for a
w
in the
\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\curlyvee}}}}\mkern 1.0mu
-class
7
7

[

]
.
.

We may omit edges which can be deduced by transitivity:

Definition 13
.

An
æ-path

in an RGB-cograph
\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathcal{G}
is an elementary path
x_{0},x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}
in the graph
\langle V,\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\frown}}}}\mkern 1.0mu\cup\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.25,0.16}\rightsquigarrow}}}}\mkern 1.0mu\cup\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\curlyvee}}}}\mkern 1.0mu\rangle
whose
edges are alternating in
\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\curlyvee}}}}\mkern 1.0mu
and in
\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.25,0.16}\rightsquigarrow}}}}\mkern 1.0mu\cup\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\frown}}}}\mkern 1.0mu
.
A
chord
in an æ-path is an edge
x_{i}\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\frown}}}}\mkern 1.0mux_{j}
or
x_{i}\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.25,0.16}\rightsquigarrow}}}}\mkern 1.0mux_{j}
for

i,j\in\{0,\dots,n\}
and
i+2\leq j
. A
chordless æ-path
is
an æ-path without chord. An
æ-cycle
is an æ-path
such that
x_{0}=x_{n}
. An RGB-cograph
\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathcal{G}
is

æ-connected
if any two vertices are connected by a chordless
æ-path,
and
\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathcal{G}
is
æ-acyclic
if it contains no chordless æ-cycle.

Connectedness and acyclicity are used to define the following notions of correctness.

Definition 14
.

We say that an RGB-cograph
\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathcal{G}
is
\mathsf{MELL}
-correct
if it satisfies the following conditions:

1.

V_{\mathcal{G}}\neq\emptyset
and
\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathcal{G}
is æ-connected and æ-acyclic;

2.

if
w\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathcal{G}}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.25,0.16}\rightsquigarrow}}}}\mkern 1.0muv
and
v\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\curlyvee}}}}\mkern 1.0muv^{\prime}
, then there is
w^{\prime}\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\curlyvee}}}}\mkern 1.0muw
such that
w^{\prime}\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathcal{G}}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.25,0.16}\rightsquigarrow}}}}\mkern 1.0muv^{\prime}
.

We say that RGB-cograph is
\mathsf{MLL}
-correct
(or
\mathsf{MLL_{u}}
-correct
)
if

\mathsf{MELL}
-correct

and

V=V^{\bullet}
(respectively
V=V^{\bullet}\cup V^{\scriptstyle{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\circ}}
)

Lemma 16

\lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}}}}F
.

Proof.

If
\mathsf{X}=\mathsf{MLL}
, then each
\mathsf{MLL}
-correct RGB-cograph is an æ-connected æ-acyclic RB-cograph, the result is proven in
[
38
,
41
,
45
]
.
The proof proceeds by induction on the size of an RB-cograph
\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathcal{G}
showing that each RB-cograph is either an
\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\curlyvee}}}}\mkern 1.0mu
-class or there is a
splitting
, that is,

V_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathcal{G}}=U\uplus V
and
if
u\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathcal{G}}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\curlyvee}}}}\mkern 1.0muv
then either
u,v\in U
or
u,v\in V
,
and there are
U^{\prime}\subset U
and
V^{\prime}\subset V
such that for all
u\in U
and
v\in V
,
u\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathcal{G}}}{{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\frown}}}}\mkern 1.0muv
iff

and
u\in V^{\prime}
.
In particular, each
\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\curlyvee}}}}\mkern 1.0mu
-class
\{a,\bar{a}\}
of a
\mathsf{MLL}
-correct RGB-cograph
\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathcal{G}
encodes an
\mathsf{ax}
-rule with conclusion

, and each splitting encodes a
\mathop{\otimes}
-rule.

If
\mathsf{X}=\mathsf{MLL_{u}}
, then the statement straightforwardly follows
the the previous result.
In this case each
\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\curlyvee}}}}\mkern 1.0mu
-class encodes either an
\mathsf{ax}_{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}j}}
-rule if it contains a pair of atomic vertices, or a
\mathsf{1}_{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}j}}

If
\mathsf{X}=\mathsf{MELL}
,
the proof strategy is to define for each
\mathsf{MELL}
-correct RGB-cograph
\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathcal{G}

Then we shall use the derivation corresponding to
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}{\partial({\mathcal{G}})}}
to reconstruct a derivation for
\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathcal{G}
.

Definition of
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}{\partial({\mathcal{G}})}}
:

We define
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}{\partial({\mathcal{G}})}}

We define a vertex set

Properties of
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}{\partial({\mathcal{G}})}}
.

The intuition behind this construction can be explained using
Theorem
7
.
Following
[
20
]
, we use the

\mathsf{BV}
-formula

In

We write

\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathcal{G}

If

\hskip-13.00005pt{\partial({F\{v_{1}\mathbin{\vartriangleleft}B_{1}\}\cdots\{v_{n}\mathbin{\vartriangleleft}B_{n}\}})}=(\bar{v}^{\prime}_{1}\mathop{\otimes}\cdots\mathop{\otimes}\bar{v}^{\prime}_{n}\mathop{\otimes}{\partial({B_{1}\invamp\cdots\invamp B_{n}})})\invamp{\partial({F\{v^{\prime}_{1}\}\cdots\{v^{\prime}_{n}\}})}

(7)

We can use (

) to construct

For this, observe that, a priori, moving a
B_{i}

However, we only claim that

Figure

12
shows two examples of the definition of
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}{\partial({\mathcal{G}})}}
.

Sequentialization of
\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathcal{G}
using
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}{\partial({\mathcal{G}})}}
.

We can now piggyback
on Retoré’s proof
[
45
]
of sequentialization for
RB-cographs, to produce an
{\mathsf{MLL}\mbox{-}{\mathsf{K}}}
sequent
proof for
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathsf{fm}(\mathcal{G})}
.
Since
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}{\partial({\mathcal{G}})}}
and each of the
{\partial({B_{1}\invamp\cdots\invamp B_{n}})}
determined by the
\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\curlyvee}}}}\mkern 1.0mu
-classes of modalities
are
æ-connected and æ-acyclic RB-cograph,
there is a splitting tensor in
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathsf{fm}({\partial({\mathcal{G}})})}

(we can remove roots
\invamp
via the
\invamp
-rule). If this splitting
tensor is also present in
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathsf{fm}(\mathcal{G})}
, we can directly apply the

\mathop{\otimes}
rule and proceed by induction hypothesis. If it is not present in
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathsf{fm}(\mathcal{G})}
then it must be of shape
\bar{v}^{\prime}_{1}\mathop{\otimes}\cdots\mathop{\otimes}\bar{v}^{\prime}_{n}\mathop{\otimes}{\partial({B_{1}\invamp\cdots\invamp B_{n}})}
and be introduced by the translation in
Equation

7
. Since
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}{\partial({\mathcal{G}})}}
is æ-connected, we can without loss of generality assume the the context consists only of
v_{1}^{\prime},\ldots,v_{n}^{\prime}
. Otherwise our tensor would not be splitting. Hence, we have

\scriptstyle-

\scriptstyle-

\scriptstyle-

\;\mathsf{ax}

v_{1}^{\prime},\bar{v}_{1}^{\prime}

\hskip 9.24994pt\cdots\hskip 9.24994pt

\scriptstyle-

\scriptstyle-

\scriptstyle-

\;\mathsf{ax}

v_{n}^{\prime},\bar{v}_{n}^{\prime}

\scriptstyle-

\scriptstyle-

\scriptstyle-

\;\mathop{\otimes}

v_{1}^{\prime},\ldots,v_{n}^{\prime},\bar{v}^{\prime}_{1}\mathop{\otimes}\cdots\mathop{\otimes}\bar{v}^{\prime}_{n}

\scriptstyle-

\scriptstyle\mskip-4.0mu\mathchar 781\mskip-4.0mu

\scriptstyle\mskip-4.0mu\mathchar 781\mskip-4.0mu

\scriptstyle\mskip-4.0mu\mathchar 781\mskip-4.0mu

\hskip 18.49988pt{\partial({B_{1}\invamp\cdots\invamp B_{n}})}

\scriptstyle-

\scriptstyle-

\scriptstyle-

\;\mathop{\otimes}

v_{1}^{\prime},\ldots,v_{n}^{\prime},\bar{v}^{\prime}_{1}\mathop{\otimes}\cdots\mathop{\otimes}\bar{v}^{\prime}_{n}\mathop{\otimes}{\partial({B_{1}\invamp\cdots\invamp B_{n}})}

(8)

whose conclusion is
\partial((v_{1}\mathbin{\vartriangleleft}B_{1})\invamp\cdots\invamp(v_{n}\mathbin{\vartriangleleft}B_{n}))
. Thus, we can apply the
\mathsf{w}\oc p
-rule and we can proceed by induction hypothesis.

Moreover, if
V^{\scriptstyle{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\circ}}_{\mathcal{G}}\neq\emptyset
, then we conclude similarly to the case of
\mathsf{MLL_{u}}
-correct RGB-cographs.
∎

We summarize the main results of this section
by means of the following theorem:

Theorem 17
.

Let
\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathcal{G}
be a RGB-cograph with
\lfloor{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathcal{G}}\rfloor={\llbracket F\rrbracket}
and
\mathsf{X}\in\{\mathsf{MLL},\mathsf{MLL_{u}},\mathsf{MELL}\}
. Then

F
provable in
\mathsf{X^{\ell}}

\iff

\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathcal{G}
is
\mathsf{X}
-correct

5
\mathsf{MELL}
-Fibrations

In this section we show how specific morphisms between modal relation webs, which we call
\mathsf{MELL}
-fibrations
, allow us encode
\mathsf{MELL}^{\downarrow}
derivations.
We here present some of the results in
[
7
]
where skew fibrations are meant to capture (deep) weakening-contraction derivations in modal logic.
In fact, thanks to additional definitions, we are able to restrain the these rules applications only to the ones on
\wn
-formulas (or
\bot
).
In the syntax proposed in this paper (deep) weakening-rules cannot properly be pushed down in the derivation since the information of the jump,
represented by the propositional constant
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\circ}
,
is firmly attached to an an axiom- or a
\mathsf{1}
-rule.
Nevertheless, we separate the instantiation of a weakening (the jump appearing in a
\mathsf{ax}_{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}j}}
- or
\mathsf{1}_{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}j}}
) from the weakening application (the
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathsf{w}_{\wn}^{\downarrow}}
- or
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\bot^{\mathsf{j}}}^{\downarrow}
-rule).

and

(11)

4.

{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}f}

preserves non-jump labels
and
assign jumps
, that is

\begin{array}[]{c@{\qquad}c}\mbox{if $l(v)\neq{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\circ}$, then $l(v)=l({\color[rgb]{1,0,1}f}(v))$;}&\mbox{if $l(v)={\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\circ}$, then $l({\color[rgb]{1,0,1}f}(v))\in\{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\circ},\bot,\wn\}$.}\end{array}

(12)

5.

{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}f}
has the
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\circ}
-domination
property, i.e.,

\begin{array}[]{c}\mbox{
if $w\in V_{\mathcal{H}}\setminus{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}f}(V_{\mathcal{G}})$, then there is a $u\in V^{\scriptstyle{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\circ}}_{\mathcal{G}}$ such that
${\color[rgb]{1,0,1}f}(u)\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.25,0.16}\rightsquigarrow}}}}\mkern 1.0muw$, $l({\color[rgb]{1,0,1}f}(u))=\wn$,
}\\
\mbox{and if ${\color[rgb]{1,0.5,0}R}\in\{\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\frown}}}}\mkern 1.0mu,\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.25,0.16}\rightsquigarrow}}}}\mkern 1.0mu\}$, then ${\color[rgb]{1,0,1}f}(v){{\color[rgb]{1,0.5,0}R}_{\mathcal{H}}}{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}f}(u)$ iff ${\color[rgb]{1,0,1}f}(v){\color[rgb]{1,0.5,0}R}_{\mathcal{H}}w$. }\end{array}

(13)

6.

{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}f}
has the
\wn
-domination
property, i.e.:

\begin{array}[]{c}\mbox{if ${\color[rgb]{1,0,1}f}(v_{1})={\color[rgb]{1,0,1}f}(v_{2})$, then there are $w_{1}\neq w_{2}$ such that ${\color[rgb]{1,0,1}f}(w_{1})={\color[rgb]{1,0,1}f}(w_{2})=w$, $l(w)=\wn$ and}\\
\begin{array}[]{c@{\qquad}|@{\qquad}c}\mbox{either }w_{1}=v_{1}\mbox{ and }w_{2}=v_{2}&\mbox{or }w_{1}\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.25,0.16}\rightsquigarrow}}}}\mkern 1.0muv_{1}\mbox{ and }w_{2}\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.25,0.16}\rightsquigarrow}}}}\mkern 1.0muv_{2}\end{array}\end{array}

(14)

The conditions in
Definition

18
have a simple interpretation if we identify the vertices of
\mathcal{G}
and
\mathcal{H}
with the atoms,
\bot
,
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\circ}
,
\wn
and
\oc
occurring in the corresponding encoded formulas
G
and
H
, and the and nodes in the formula trees of
G
and
H
.
In fact, there is a
\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\frown}}}}\mkern 1.0mu
between two vertices iff their least common ancestor in the formula tree is a
\mathop{\otimes}
.
Similarly, there is a
\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.25,0.16}\rightsquigarrow}}}}\mkern 1.0mu
from a vertex
v
to a vertex
w
iff
w
is an atom in the scope of a modality
v
; more precisely,
v
is the least common ancestor of
v
and
w
.
According with this remark the above conditions have the following interpretation:

1.

a linear fibration does not modify the least common ancestor of the corresponding nodes in the formula tree;

2.

if the image of a vertex
u
is a modality dominating the image of a vertex
v
, then there is a vertex
w
with the same image of
u
such that it is a modality dominating
v
;

3.

a skew fibration can replace an internal node
n
by a disjunction node with one child
n
and the other child any formula tree;
a skew fibration can attach a formula tree below a node of a modality with no child;

4.

all labels except the
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\circ}
are preserved by
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}f}
. If
l(v)
, then
l({\color[rgb]{1,0,1}f}(v))
may be preserved or become either a
\bot
or a
\wn
;

5.

if a vertex in
\mathcal{H}
is not image of a vertex in
\mathcal{G}
, then there is a target of a
\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.25,0.16}\rightsquigarrow}}}}\mkern 1.0mu
with source a vertex
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}f}(u)
with such that
l({\color[rgb]{1,0,1}f}(u))=\wn
and
l(u)={\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\circ}
;

6.

if a vertex
v
of
\mathcal{H}
is the image of
n>1
distinct vertices
v_{1},\dots,v_{n}
in
\mathcal{G}
, then each of these vertices is an atom or a modality of a formula of the shape
\wn A
.

\Gamma\{A\mathop{\otimes}(B\mathop{\otimes}C)\}

\scriptstyle-

\scriptstyle-

\scriptstyle-

\;\equiv

\Gamma\{(A\mathop{\otimes}B)\mathop{\otimes}C\}

\Gamma\{A\invamp(B\invamp C)\}

\scriptstyle-

\scriptstyle-

\scriptstyle-

\;\equiv

\Gamma\{(A\invamp B)\invamp C\}

\Gamma\{B\mathop{\otimes}A\}

\scriptstyle-

\scriptstyle-

\scriptstyle-

\;\equiv

\Gamma\{A\mathop{\otimes}B\}

\Gamma\{B\invamp A\}

\scriptstyle-

\scriptstyle-

\scriptstyle-

\;\equiv

\Gamma\{A\invamp B\}

Figure 13:
Deep rules for formula equivalence.

These conditions allow us to restraint the correspondence between contractions-weakening derivations and skew fibrations
[
24
,
47
,
7
,
6
,
35
]
on the formulas on the form
\wn A
.
However, since in relation web we consider formulas modulo associativity and commutativity of
\mathop{\otimes}
and
\invamp
(see
Proposition

11
), we need to also consider the additional (deep) rules in
Figure

13
taking care of this equivalence.

Proposition 19
.

If
\Gamma
and
\Gamma^{\prime}
are sequents, then

Definition 20
.

We say that two vertices

{\color[rgb]{1,0.5,0}R}\in\{\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\frown}}}}\mkern 1.0mu,\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.25,0.16}\rightsquigarrow}}}}\mkern 1.0mu,\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.25,0.16}\leftsquigarrow}}}}\mkern 1.0mu,\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{{\smile}}}}\mkern 1.0mu\}

{}{}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{}\lxSVG@stroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 0 -3.94 L 0 3.94}{fill:none} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
\lxSVG@closescope }
\lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}}}}\Gamma
.
We conclude since, by definition, a
\mathsf{MELL}
-fibration is the composition of a
\wn
-map and a linear fibration.

To prove the converse, we define the relation web
\mathcal{H}^{\prime}
such that
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}f}={\color[rgb]{1,0,1}f}^{\prime}\circ{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}f}^{\prime\prime}
with
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}f}^{\prime\prime}\colon\mathcal{H}\to\mathcal{H}^{\prime}
and
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}f}^{\prime}\colon\mathcal{H}^{\prime}\to\mathcal{G}
.
We construct
\mathcal{H}^{\prime}
from
\mathcal{H}
as follows:

•

for each pair of clones
v
and
w
with
v\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.25,0.16}\rightsquigarrow}}}}\mkern 1.0muw
in
\mathcal{H}
such that
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}f}(v)={\color[rgb]{1,0,1}f}(w)
, remove
v
;

•

if
w\in V_{\mathcal{G}}
such that
w\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.25,0.16}\rightsquigarrow}}}}\mkern 1.0mu{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}f}(v)
for some
v\in V_{\mathcal{H}}
and
w={\color[rgb]{1,0,1}f}(u)
for no
u\in V_{\mathcal{H}}
, then add
w
to
\mathcal{H}
ad all needed edges such that
w{\color[rgb]{1,0.5,0}R}_{\mathcal{H}^{\prime}}v
iff
w{\color[rgb]{1,0.5,0}R}_{\mathcal{G}}{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}f}(v)
for
{\color[rgb]{1,0.5,0}R}\in\{\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\frown}}}}\mkern 1.0mu,\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.25,0.16}\rightsquigarrow}}}}\mkern 1.0mu\}
.

We define
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}f}^{\prime\prime}
as the identity over non-clones vertices and as
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}f}
on clones vertices. We define
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}f}^{\prime}
in such a way
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}f}={\color[rgb]{1,0,1}f}^{\prime}\circ{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}f}^{\prime\prime}
. By definition
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}f}^{\prime\prime}
is a
\wn
-map and
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}f}^{\prime}
is a linear fibration.
∎

Proposition 24
.

If
\mathcal{H}
and
\mathcal{G}
are relation webs and
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}f}\colon\mathcal{H}\to\mathcal{G}
a function from
V_{\mathcal{H}}
to
V_{\mathcal{G}}
, then it can be decided if
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}f}
is a
\mathsf{MELL}
-fibration in time polynomial in
\left|\mathcal{G}\right|+\left|\mathcal{H}\right|
.

Proof.

We decompose
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}f}={\color[rgb]{1,0,1}f}^{\prime}\circ{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}f}^{\prime\prime}
using the same procedure used in the proof of
Theorem

23
.
To check if
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}f}^{\prime\prime}
is a
\wn
-map we have to check if the label of all vertices which are not in the image of
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}f}^{\prime\prime}
are
\wn
, and to check if the vertices with the same image are clones. This requires a quadratic time on the size of
V_{\mathcal{G}}
.
Similarly, checking if
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}f}^{\prime}
is a linear fibration is quadratic on the size of
\mathcal{H}^{\prime}
, which is bounded by
\left|V_{\mathcal{H}}\right|+\left|V_{\mathcal{G}}\right|
.
∎

6
Combinatorial Proofs

In this section we present a combinatorial proof syntax for
\mathsf{MELL^{j}}
using the results in the previous sections.
In particular,
Theorem

5
gives us a decomposition result allowing us
to separate in
\mathsf{MELL^{j}}
derivation,
the linear part, that is,
\mathsf{MELL}^{\ell}
,
form the resource management part, that is,
\mathsf{MELL}^{\downarrow}
.
The first part of the proof is encoded by RGB-cographs, while the second by
\mathsf{MELL}
-fibrations.

Definition 25
.

A map
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}f}\colon\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathcal{G}\to{\llbracket F\rrbracket}
from an RGB-cograph
\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathcal{G}
to
a the relation web
{\llbracket F\rrbracket}
is

allegiant
if the following conditions are satisfied:

•

if
v,w\in V^{\bullet}_{\mathcal{G}}
and
v\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathcal{G}}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\curlyvee}}}}\mkern 1.0muw
then
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}f}(v)
and
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}f}(w)
are labeled by dual atoms in
\mathcal{A}
;

•

if
v\in V_{\mathcal{G}}\setminus V^{\scriptstyle{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\circ}}_{\mathcal{G}}
then
l({\color[rgb]{1,0,1}f}(v))=l(v)
;

•

if
v\in V^{\scriptstyle{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\circ}}_{\mathcal{G}}
then
l({\color[rgb]{1,0,1}f}(v))\in\{\bot,\wn\}
.

Definition 26
.

For
\mathsf{X}\in\{\mathsf{MLL},\mathsf{MLL_{u}},\mathsf{MELL}\}
, an
\mathsf{X}
-combinatorial proof
of a sequent
\Gamma
is an
\mathsf{X}
-fibration

{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}f}\colon\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathcal{G}\to{\llbracket\Gamma\rrbracket}
from an
\mathsf{X}
-correct RGB-cograph
\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathcal{G}
to the relation web of
\Gamma
.

Theorem 27

After the result in
[
7
]
we have that
\mathsf{MELL}
-combinatorial proofs represent two
\simeq_{\mathsf{J}}
-equivalent proofs with the same syntactic object.

Proposition 28
.

Let
\pi_{1}
and
\pi_{2}
be two derivations in
\mathsf{MELL^{j}}
, then

\pi_{1}\simeq_{\mathsf{J}}\pi_{2}
iff they are represented by the same
\mathsf{MELL}
-combinatorial proof.

Proof.

It follows by the fact that
\mathsf{MELL^{j}}
can be seen as modal logic
\mathsf{S4}
with additional axiom-like rules (
\mathsf{ax}_{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}j}}
and
\mathsf{1}_{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}j}}
) and restricted versions of weakening and contraction rule.
Note that, in
[
7
]
the proof equivalence is stated in such a way rule that permutations of
\mathsf{W}
and
\mathsf{C}
below
\mathsf{w}\oc p
are not allowed.
∎

In particular, there is a one-to-one correspondence between
\mathsf{MLL_{u}}
-combinatorial proofs and
\mathsf{MLL_{u}}
proof nets with jumps in
[
23
]
.

Theorem 29
.

For all
\mathsf{X}\in\{\mathsf{MLL},\mathsf{MLL_{u}},\mathsf{MELL}\}
,
\mathsf{X}
-combinatorial proofs are a sound and complete proof system for
\mathsf{X}
in the sense of
[
10
]
.

Proof.

Let
\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathcal{G}=\langle V_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathcal{G}},\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathcal{G}}}{{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\frown}}}}\mkern 1.0mu,\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathcal{G}}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.25,0.16}\rightsquigarrow}}}}\mkern 1.0mu,\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathcal{G}}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\curlyvee}}}}\mkern 1.0mu\rangle
be a labeled mixed graph equipped with an equivalence relation,
\mathcal{H}=\langle V_{\mathcal{H}},\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathcal{H}}}{{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\frown}}}}\mkern 1.0mu,\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathcal{H}}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.25,0.16}\rightsquigarrow}}}}\mkern 1.0mu\rangle
be a labeled mixed graph and
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}f}\colon\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathcal{G}\to\mathcal{H}
mapping vertices of
\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathcal{G}
to vertices of
\mathcal{H}
.
Checking if the two mixed graphs are relation web is polynomial by
Proposition

10
on the sizes of
\left|V_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathcal{G}}\right|+\left|V_{\mathcal{H}}\right|
and checking if
\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathcal{G}
is an
\mathsf{X}
-correct RGB-cograph is polynomial on
\left|V_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathcal{G}}\right|
.
By
Proposition

24
we have that checking if
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}f}
is a
\mathsf{X}
-fibration is polynomial on
\left|V_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathcal{G}}\right|+\left|V_{\mathcal{H}}\right|
.
Then, since checking if
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}f}
is allegiant is linear on
\left|V_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathcal{G}}\right|+\left|V_{\mathcal{H}}\right|
, we conclude the proof.
∎

7
Handsome Proof Nets for
\mathsf{MELL}

The combinatorial proofs defined in the previous section can be interpreted as an extension of both Retoré’s
[
45
]
and Hughes’
[
24
]
syntaxes.
They only allow to represent
\mathsf{cut}
-free proofs as
unfolded
Retoré’s proof nets
[
41
]
do.
In this section we define
exponentially handsome proof nets
(or
\mathsf{MELL}
-combinatorial proofs with cuts
) by extending
\mathsf{MELL}
-combinatorial proofs.
We conclude by providing a cut-elimination procedure for exponentially handsome proof nets.

We adapt the solution proposed in
[
24
,
25
]
where instances of
\mathsf{cut}
are replaced by conjunction rules producing
contradictions
, i.e. formulas of the form
A\mathop{\otimes}\bar{A}
, which are later “discarded” at the end of the derivation.
In the classical setting, this substitution creates no further interaction of the contradiction with any other rule in the derivation.
The presence of the weak promotion rule prevents us from ignoring the presence of these contradictions, but we here propose a solution for this problem.

Remark 30
.

Another extension of combinatorial proof for classical logic allowing to represent proofs with cuts is given in
[
48
]
by means of
combinatorial flows
.
In this setting
\mathsf{cut}
is in some way encoded as sequential composition of flows.
This syntax is strongly related with the property of the deep inference system
\mathsf{SKS}
for classical logic
[
20
]
which states that if
\mathrel{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathsf{SKS}}}{{\hbox to15.43pt{\vbox to6.09pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 0.59999pt\lower-3.04544pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{}{{}}{}
{}{}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{}\lxSVG@stroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 0 0 L 19.69 0}{fill:none} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
\lxSVG@closescope {}{{}}{}
{}{}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{}\lxSVG@stroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 0 -3.94 L 0 3.94}{fill:none} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
\lxSVG@closescope }
\lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}}}}\bar{A}\invamp B
, then
A\mathrel{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathsf{SKS}}}{{\hbox to15.43pt{\vbox to6.09pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 0.59999pt\lower-3.04544pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{}{{}}{}
{}{}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{}\lxSVG@stroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 0 0 L 19.69 0}{fill:none} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
\lxSVG@closescope {}{{}}{}
{}{}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{}\lxSVG@stroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 0 -3.94 L 0 3.94}{fill:none} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
\lxSVG@closescope }
\lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}}}}B
.
Such a result is out of the scope of this paper, but it could be obtained by defining a deep inference system for
\mathsf{MELL^{j}}
based on the systems in
[
46
,
49
]
.

Definition 31
.

If
F
is a formula, we write
\wn^{n}F
to denote the formula
\smash{\wn^{n}F=\overbrace{\wn\cdots\wn}^{\mbox{\tiny$n$ times }}F}
. In particular,
\wn^{0}F=F
.
A
contradiction
is a formula of the form
C=A\mathop{\otimes}\bar{A}
for a
\mathsf{MELL}
-formula
A
, and a
weaken-contradiction
is a formula of the form

with

a contradiction.

.

\lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}}}}\Gamma,C_{1},\dots,C_{n}

then

\mathrel{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathsf{MELL}}}{{\hbox to15.43pt{\vbox to6.09pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 0.59999pt\lower-3.04544pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{}{{}}{}

.
Conversely, if

occurrences of the
\mathsf{cut}
-rule with pairs of active formulas
(A_{1},\bar{A}_{1}),\dots,(A_{k},\bar{A}_{k})
then

\mathrel{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathsf{MELL}}}{{\hbox to15.43pt{\vbox to6.09pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 0.59999pt\lower-3.04544pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{}{{}}{}
{}{}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{}\lxSVG@stroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 0 0 L 19.69 0}{fill:none} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
\lxSVG@closescope {}{{}}{}
{}{}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{}\lxSVG@stroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 0 -3.94 L 0 3.94}{fill:none} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
\lxSVG@closescope }
\lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}}}}\Gamma,\wn^{n_{1}}(A_{1}\mathop{\otimes}\bar{A}_{1}),\dots,\wn^{n_{k}}(A_{i}\mathop{\otimes}\bar{A}_{i})

for some
n_{1},\dots,n_{k}\in\mathbb{N}
.

Proof.

By induction on the number of weaken-contradictions formulas
k
.
If
\Gamma,C
is provable in
\mathsf{MELL}
and
C=\wn^{n}(A\mathop{\otimes}\bar{A})
, then in any derivation of
\Gamma,C
there is an occurrence of a rule
\mathop{\otimes}
with principal formula
A\mathop{\otimes}\bar{A}
and active formulas
A
and
\bar{A}
.
We can obtain a derivation of
\Gamma
by replacing such an occurrence with a
\mathsf{cut}
having the same active formulas, and then removing each occurrence of the active formula
A\mathop{\otimes}\bar{A}
from the derivation.

{{}{}\vbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\vbox{\hbox{\hbox{\hbox{\hbox{\hbox{$\Gamma,A$}\kern 10.00002pt}\hbox{$\bar{A},\Delta$}}}}\kern 1.43518pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox to0.0pt{\hss\hbox{$\smash{\lower 2.5pt\hbox{$$}}$}}\vbox{\vbox to0.4pt{\vfill\hbox to45.97224pt{\vbox to0.0pt{\vss\hbox{$\scriptstyle-$}\vss}\hss\leaders{\vbox to0.0pt{\vss\hbox{\kern-1.3pt\vbox to0.0pt{\vss\hbox{$\scriptstyle-$}\vss}\kern-1.3pt}\vss}}{\hskip 40.05562pt}\hss\vbox to0.0pt{\vss\hbox{$\scriptstyle-$}\vss}}\vfill}}\hbox to0.0pt{\hbox{$\smash{\lower 2.5pt\hbox{$\;\mathop{\otimes}$}}$}\hss}\kern 0.0pt}\kern 1.43518pt\hbox{\kern 1.1111pt\hbox{$\Gamma,A\mathop{\otimes}\bar{A},\Delta$}\kern 1.1111pt}}}\kern 10.55551pt}}}\qquad\leftrightsquigarrow\qquad{{}{}\vbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\vbox{\hbox{\hbox{\hbox{\hbox{\hbox{$\Gamma,A$}\kern 10.00002pt}\hbox{$\bar{A},\Delta$}}}}\kern 1.43518pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox to0.0pt{\hss\hbox{$\smash{\lower 2.5pt\hbox{$$}}$}}\vbox{\vbox to0.4pt{\vfill\hbox to45.97224pt{\vbox to0.0pt{\vss\hbox{$\scriptstyle-$}\vss}\hss\leaders{\vbox to0.0pt{\vss\hbox{\kern-1.3pt\vbox to0.0pt{\vss\hbox{$\scriptstyle-$}\vss}\kern-1.3pt}\vss}}{\hskip 40.05562pt}\hss\vbox to0.0pt{\vss\hbox{$\scriptstyle-$}\vss}}\vfill}}\hbox to0.0pt{\hbox{$\smash{\lower 2.5pt\hbox{$\;\mathsf{cut}$}}$}\hss}\kern 0.0pt}\kern 1.43518pt\hbox{\kern 13.47223pt\hbox{$\Gamma,\Delta$}\kern 13.47223pt}}}\kern 15.99994pt}}}

Then we conclude thanks to
Theorem

1
.

The converse is proven by similarly.
In this case
n_{i}
is defined as the number of occurrences of
\mathsf{w}\oc p
below the
\mathsf{cut}
with active formulas formula
A_{i}
and
\bar{A}_{i}
for each
i\in\{1,\dots k\}
.
∎

Definition 33
.

An
exponentially handsome proof net
of a sequent
\Gamma
is a
\mathsf{MELL}
-combinatorial proof
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}f}\colon{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathcal{G}}\to{\llbracket\Gamma,\Delta\rrbracket}
where
\Delta
is a (possibly empty) sequent of weaken-contradictions.

In drawing such objects, we shade in gray the backgrounds of the portion of the relation web of
\Gamma
containing the vertices of the weaken-contradictions (for a graphical example refer to
Figure

1
).

We conclude this section by defining a graphical rewriting allowing us to produce a
\mathsf{MELL}
-combinatorial proof from an exponentially handsome proof net.

Theorem 34
.

If
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}f}\colon{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathcal{G}}\to{\llbracket\Gamma,\Delta\rrbracket}
is an exponentially handsome proof nets of
\Gamma
, then there is a
\mathsf{MELL}
-combinatorial proof
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}f}^{\prime}\colon{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathcal{G}}\to{\llbracket\Gamma\rrbracket}
.

Proof.

If
\Delta=\emptyset
, then
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}f}
is a
\mathsf{MELL}
-combinatorial proof.
Otherwise, in order prove this result we implement cut-elimination by translating the rewriting in
Figure

8
.
We consider the following key cases which are shown in
Figure

14
:

•

\overset{\mathsf{ax}\mbox{-VS-}\mathsf{ax}}{\rightsquigarrow_{\mathsf{cut}}}
:
remove the two vertices in the contradiction and merge their
\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\curlyvee}}}}\mkern 1.0mu
-classes;

•

\overset{\bot\mbox{-VS-}\mathsf{1}}{\rightsquigarrow_{\mathsf{cut}}}
:
similarly to the previous one;

•

\overset{\mathop{\otimes}\mbox{-VS-}\invamp}{\rightsquigarrow_{\mathsf{cut}}}
:
remove the
\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\frown}}}}\mkern 1.0mu
-edges between the vertices in
B
and the ones in
A
and
\bar{A}
, and remove the
\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\frown}}}}\mkern 1.0mu
-edges between the vertices in
A
and the ones in
\bar{B}
;

•

\overset{\mathsf{w}\oc p\mbox{-VS-}\mathsf{w}\oc p}{\rightsquigarrow_{\mathsf{cut}}}
:
replace the
\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\frown}}}}\mkern 1.0mu
-edges between
\wn
and a vertex in
A
with
\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.25,0.16}\rightsquigarrow}}}}\mkern 1.0mu
-edge from
\wn
to a vertex in
A
.
Merge the
\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\curlyvee}}}}\mkern 1.0mu
-classes of
\oc
and
\wn
and then remove the vertex
\oc
;

•

\overset{\mathsf{w}\oc p\mbox{-VS-}\mathsf{der}_{\wn}}{\rightsquigarrow_{\mathsf{cut}}}
:
remove the
\oc
and the vertices in its
\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\curlyvee}}}}\mkern 1.0mu
-class;

•

\overset{\mathsf{w}\oc p\mbox{-VS-}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathsf{w^{j}}}}{\rightsquigarrow_{\mathsf{cut}}}
:
remove the
\oc
and any vertex pointed by the
\wn
in its
\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\curlyvee}}}}\mkern 1.0mu
-class.
Then replace each
\wn
in with a new
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\circ}
having the same image by
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}f}
.
Add to the
\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\curlyvee}}}}\mkern 1.0mu
-class of the
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\circ}^{\mathsf{cut}}
which is in the pre-image of the
\wn
of the cut-formula the new
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\circ}
-vertices.
Finally remove
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\circ}^{\mathsf{cut}}
.

•

\overset{\mathsf{w}\oc p\mbox{-VS-}\mathsf{c}_{\wn}}{\rightsquigarrow_{\mathsf{cut}}}
:
remove any
\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\frown}}}}\mkern 1.0mu
connecting
\oc A
to any copy of
\wn\bar{A}
;
for each pre-mage of
\wn
excepting one, make a copy of the connected component of the RGB-cograph containing the
\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\curlyvee}}}}\mkern 1.0mu
-class of
\oc

for each
\wn
in the pre-image of the
\wn
of the cut-formula
\wn\bar{A}
.
add the
\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\frown}}}}\mkern 1.0mu
-edges between each copy of
\oc A
and the corresponding copy of
\wn\bar{A}
;

•

\overset{\mathsf{w}\oc p\mbox{-VS-}\mathsf{dig}_{\wn}}{\rightsquigarrow_{\mathsf{cut}}}
:
remove any
\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\frown}}}}\mkern 1.0mu
connecting
\oc A
to any
\wn
with image the
\wn
of the cut-formula;
make a copy of the
\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\curlyvee}}}}\mkern 1.0mu
-class of
\oc
for each
\wn
in the pre-image of the
\wn
of the cut-formula
\wn\bar{A}
.
Add the
\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\frown}}}}\mkern 1.0mu
-edge and the
\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.25,0.16}\rightsquigarrow}}}}\mkern 1.0mu
-edges in such a way each new copy of
\wn
and
\oc
is a clone of the original one.
Add a
\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\frown}}}}\mkern 1.0mu
between each new copy of
\oc
and the corresponding
\wn
.

Note that proof equivalence and the permutations in
Figure

9
are already captured by the syntax.

Let
\Delta=C_{1},\dots,C_{n}
.
We define the function
\mathsf{W}_{\Delta}
associating to an exponentially handsome proof nets
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}g}\colon{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathcal{H}}\to{\llbracket\Sigma\rrbracket}
the string
\mathsf{W}_{\Delta}({\color[rgb]{1,0,1}g})=(\left|\Sigma\right|_{C_{1}},\dots,\left|\Sigma\right|_{C_{n}})
where
\left|\Sigma\right|_{C}
is the number of occurrences of the the formula
C
in
\Sigma
.
The reduction strategy consists in selecting and applying reduction to one weaken-contradiction in
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}f}
at a time, selecting the weaken-contradictions according with the following the order on
\Delta
: we do not select a weaken-contradiction
C_{i+1}
until we have not removed all the occurrences of
C_{i}
.
At the end of each sub-routine removing an occurrence of a weaken-contradiction
C_{i}
, we may have created new copies of the weaken-contradictions, but only copies of the
C_{j}
with
j>i
.
The reduction order is the lexicographic order on the pair
(\left|V_{{\llbracket C\rrbracket}}\right|,\mathsf{W}_{\Delta}({\color[rgb]{1,0,1}g}))
where
C
is the currently selected weaken-contradiction in the elimination process.
Since each rewriting rule in
Figure

14
either reduces
\left|{\llbracket C\rrbracket}\right|
or
\mathsf{W}_{\Delta}
, then the cut-elimination procedure ends.
∎
