Cut-elimination steps for exponentially handsome proof nets. Dotted lines delimit modules, that is, sets of vertices having the same
\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\frown}}}}\mkern 1.0mu
- and
\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.25,0.16}\rightsquigarrow}}}}\mkern 1.0mu
-relation with any vertex outside.
To simplify the reading we write with the same symbol a formula and its pre-image by
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}f}
.

8
Conclusions

In this paper we extended Retoré’s RB-cograph syntax for multiplicative proof nets
[
45
]
in order to include units and exponentials,
refining the combinatorial proofs for modal logic from
[
7
]
.

Aware of the limits in designing a syntax able to capture proof equivalence and with a polynomial correctness criterion
[
22
]
, we restrained the notion of proof equivalence
by introducing the proof system
\mathsf{MELL^{j}}
for
\mathsf{MELL}
, enforcing a coarser proof equivalence.
We topologically characterized
mixed graphs equipped with vertices partitions encoding linear proofs in
\mathsf{MELL^{j}}
,
as well as the graph homomorphisms capturing the resource management part of proofs in
\mathsf{MELL^{j}}
.
Using these results we introduced combinatorial proofs for
\mathsf{MELL}
and then exponentially handsome proof nets for
\mathsf{MELL}
, defined as compositions of combinatorial proofs.
We also provided a normalization procedure by means of graph rewriting rules.

The RGB-cographs can be interpreted as a
coherent interaction graphs
[
34
]
for
\mathsf{MLL}\cup\{\mathsf{w}\oc p\}
.
We foresee a further application of exponentially handsome proof nets to explore the geometry of interaction of
\mathsf{MELL}

[
17
]
using the same approach from
[
15
]
,
where handsome proof nets are employed to investigate coherent spaces of
\mathsf{MLL}
.

On Removing Jumps.

Is it possible to modify exponentially handsome proof nets by removing jumps and thus recover a less coarse notion of proof equivalence including jump rewiring, at the price of loosing the polynomiality of the correctness criterion.

For this purpose,
we should consider the following set of rules:

\{\mathsf{ax},\mathsf{1},{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\circ},\invamp,\mathop{\otimes},\mathsf{mix},\mathsf{w}\oc p,\mathsf{der}_{\wn},\mathsf{dig}_{\wn},\mathsf{dig}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\circ},{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\bot^{\mathsf{j}}},{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathsf{w^{j}}},\mathsf{c}_{\wn}\}\qquad\mbox{ with }\qquad{}\smash{{{}{}\vbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\vbox{\hbox{\hbox{\hbox{\hbox{\hbox{$\Gamma$}\kern 10.00002pt}\hbox{$\Delta$}}}}\kern 1.43518pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox to0.0pt{\hss\hbox{$\smash{\lower 2.5pt\hbox{$$}}$}}\vbox{\vbox to0.4pt{\vfill\hbox to24.58339pt{\vbox to0.0pt{\vss\hbox{$\scriptstyle-$}\vss}\hss\leaders{\vbox to0.0pt{\vss\hbox{\kern-1.3pt\vbox to0.0pt{\vss\hbox{$\scriptstyle-$}\vss}\kern-1.3pt}\vss}}{\hskip 18.66676pt}\hss\vbox to0.0pt{\vss\hbox{$\scriptstyle-$}\vss}}\vfill}}\hbox to0.0pt{\hbox{$\smash{\lower 2.5pt\hbox{$\;\mathsf{mix}$}}$}\hss}\kern 0.0pt}\kern 1.43518pt\hbox{\kern 2.7778pt\hbox{$\Gamma,\Delta$}\kern 2.7778pt}}}\kern 17.72218pt}}}}\qquad\mbox{ and }\qquad{}\smash{{\vbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\vbox{\hbox{\kern 3.61108pt\hbox{\hbox{$$}}\kern 3.61108pt}\kern 1.43518pt\hbox{\hbox to0.0pt{\hss\hbox{$\smash{\lower 2.5pt\hbox{$$}}$}}\vbox{\vbox to0.4pt{\vfill\hbox to7.22218pt{\vbox to0.0pt{\vss\hbox{$\scriptstyle-$}\vss}\hss\leaders{\vbox to0.0pt{\vss\hbox{\kern-1.3pt\vbox to0.0pt{\vss\hbox{$\scriptstyle-$}\vss}\kern-1.3pt}\vss}}{\hskip 1.30556pt}\hss\vbox to0.0pt{\vss\hbox{$\scriptstyle-$}\vss}}\vfill}}\hbox to0.0pt{\hbox{$\smash{\lower 2.5pt\hbox{$\;{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\circ}$}}$}\hss}}\kern 1.43518pt\hbox{\hbox{$\kern 1.38892pt\hbox{${\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\circ}$}\kern 1.38892pt$}}}}\kern 9.9999pt}}}}

A correctness criterion for RGB-cographs encoding linear proofs of this proof system,
that is, derivations containing only rules in
\{\mathsf{ax},\mathsf{1},{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\circ},\invamp,\mathop{\otimes},\mathsf{mix},\mathsf{w}\oc p\}
,
is obtained by dropping the æ-connectness from
14
.

Note that we cannot get rid of
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\circ}
in presence of the restricted weakening rule of linear logic: without placeholders we could not represent the proof below on the left, because the skew lifting condition (see
Equation

10
) would fail for any
\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\frown}}}}\mkern 1.0mu
-edge connecting a vertex in
A
with a vertex in
B
.

On Generalized
\wn
-Nodes.

The rule permutations allowing to push weakening and contraction below the promotion rule (see last line of
Figure

5
) are allowed in
\mathsf{MELL}
proof nets, thanks to the so-called
generalized
\wn
-nodes

[
11
]
.
The syntax with generalized
\wn
-nodes captures these equivalences, allowing a “flexible” representation of boxes, which are the syntactic elements representing promotion rules.
In fact, generalized
\wn
-nodes allow to identify nets where boxes may have different amounts of auxiliary ports.
This depends on the fact that boxes have a different status with respect to the interaction net syntax
[
28
]
.

In exponentially handsome proof nets, each (weak) promotion is rigidly encoded: each
\oc
-vertex is the principal port of a box and each auxiliary port is encoded by a
\wn
-vertex in the same
\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\curlyvee}}}}\mkern 1.0mu
-class.
In particular, this allows us to keep track of the depth of a propositional letter
a
, a
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\circ}
or a
\mathsf{1}
in terms of the number of incoming
\mkern 1.0mu\mathord{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.25,0.16}\rightsquigarrow}}}}\mkern 1.0mu
in the RGB-cograph.
This clearly prevents any rule permutation which may change the number of auxiliary ports of a box.
